title: Back to the source
hookLine: ninth picture: rivers flow, flowers bloom, just as they are
last: LET GO OF THE SEEKER TOO.

cards: After the empty circle, you might expect something grand: light, gold, a figure on a lotus. The ninth picture shows a river. A tree on its bank, a few flowers, water moving past rocks.
No herdsman, no ox, no circle. It looks like a page from any landscape painter's sketchbook. That's the surprise.
After all that searching and letting go, the picture comes back to the plain, ordinary world, seen clearly.

teach.b: First, pure from the beginning. The preface says, in paraphrase, that from the start things have been pure, with no dust on them. Nothing had to be built or added.
The herdsman went through every stage only to see what was already the case.

teach.h: SO MANY STEPS TO GET BACK.
teach.b: Second, so many steps to get back. The verse has a line that's almost funny, in paraphrase: so many steps to return to the root, it would have been better to be blind and deaf from the start. The journey wasn't wasted.
He arrives where he always stood, like coming home from a long trip and seeing your own street as if for the first time. Third, things as they are.

teach.h: THE RIVER FLOWS, THE FLOWERS ARE RED.
teach.b: The verse ends with the river flowing on, quietly, and the flowers simply red. The preface adds that the water is green and the mountains blue. No symbolism.
The river isn't a metaphor for time; the flowers aren't about beauty fading. A river and flowers, and that's enough.
Fourth, watching without grabbing. The preface says he sits in stillness and watches things come together and come apart, without being caught by them.
The empty circle didn't erase the world. It cleared away the reaching, and the world comes back, not as a problem to solve or a prize to win, but as it is. In this reading, the source isn't far away.
It's a river on a Tuesday afternoon.

how: Zen teachers point to the ninth oxherding picture to show that awakening, as this series describes it, returns to ordinary life rather than leaving it, and some teachers invite students to sit or walk outdoors and simply look.

games.q: what does “back to the source” mean?
o: a hidden heaven far beyond the ordinary world
the plain world seen clearly, just as it always was
a symbol: the river is time, the flower fading beauty

games.q: back to the source: tap the pairs.

s: the ninth picture shows the herdsman glowing with light
there's no herdsman at all; just a river and flowers.
the verse says the return to the root was effort spent for nothing
it says it would have been better to be blind and deaf from the start.
in this picture the river stands for the passing of time
the point is the river as it is, with no symbol pinned to it.

games.q: after the empty circle, you're asked to paint the ninth picture. what does the series actually show?
o: a golden figure seated on a lotus.
a river and flowering tree, just as they are.
the ox returning with the herdsman.
games.why: the ninth picture is a plain landscape. the series comes back to the ordinary world, seen clearly, with nothing added.

practice: Let your eyes rest on something living or moving: a tree outside the window, a plant on a shelf, clouds, even the light on a wall. Don't name it, admire it or turn it into a lesson; let it be green, or moving, or still.
When the mind starts commenting, come back to looking.

wordCard.voice: Back to the source. The ninth oxherding picture: no herdsman, no ox, only a river and flowers, the world seen just as it is, as it was all along. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese (fanben huanyuan): 'returning to the root, going back to the source', the name of the ninth oxherding picture.

carryVoice: Your line: just as it is. The river flows on, and the flowers are simply red. Back tomorrow, same hill.
